Loop Or Halt

AlgorithmsInductionLogic
Game: A row of numbers is shuffled. Look at the first number, say 3, and flip the first 3 numbers around. Keep going and see whether it ever stops.
How to play: Pick how long the row is and press New row. The page shows every flip, one under the other, until 1 is first.

    Look for the math

    A process with only finitely many possible states must either stop or repeat itself forever. Here the states are the arrangements of the numbers, so the question is real: could the flipping go round in a loop? It never does, and the reason is a small, neat argument.

    The largest leader leads only once

    Look at the numbers that come first (the leaders, shown under the rows). Let L be the largest of them. When L leads, the first L numbers are flipped, so L lands in place L. To lead again it would have to be moved out of that place, but only a larger leader could do that, and L is the largest. So L leads exactly once. The test confirmed this for every one of the 362,880 starting rows of length 9 (and every shorter length).

    Then it gets smaller

    After L has led, every later leader is smaller than L. Apply the same argument to the largest of those, and so on. The largest leader falls every round, like a descent that cannot go on for ever, and the only place it can end is 1. The test checked that every later leader is smaller, and that every row halts with 1 first.

    How long can it take?

    The proof gives no count of the steps. The test found the longest run over all starting rows: 2, 4, 7, 10, 16, 22, 30 flips for lengths 3 to 9. It grows quickly. With cards instead of numbers this process is known as Topswops.

    Press New row several times at length 12. Do the leaders ever repeat? Which is the largest leader, and does it lead only once?
